articles.title: China calls on US to end blockade on Cuba and respect its sovereignty
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: A day after joining the overwhelming majority of countries in the UN General Assembly to vote on a resolution demanding the lifting of the US blockade and sanctions on Cuba, China called on the US to immediately stop its threats of force against the country. “The illegal economic embargo and unilateral economic sanctions imposed by the US against Cuba have lasted for 64 years inflicting untold suffering on Cuban people,” Guo Jiakun, official spokesperson of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said during a regular press conference on Thursday, October 29. Claiming that “the overwhelming majority of countries in the world are outraged by the US’s serious violation of the purposes and principles of the UN Charter,” China reiterated the “international community’s longstanding call for the US to immediately stop infringing on the Cuban people’s right to survive and thrive.” On Wednesday, 130 countries voted in favor of a resolution in the UN General Assembly demanding the end of decades of unilateral US sanctions and blockade on Cuba. This was the 34th consecutive time since 1992 that the UNGA had adopted the resolution holding the US responsible for violating Cuba’s right to self-determination and other international laws. Though the US embargo and unilateral sanctions against Cuba are decades old, they have intensified since Donald Trump came to power for the second term last year. The economic blockade has particularly created massive shortages of essential goods and services such as fuel, electricity, food, and medicine, affecting millions on the island nation. The embargo has caused disruptions in medical services and impacted basic sectors of the Cuban economy, rendering thousands of people jobless, with the UN warning of “humanitarian collapse” if it continues. Cuba has claimed that US sanctions and embargoes cause over eight billion in losses to the country’s economy every year. Some countries, including China, have tried to assist Cuba by providing humanitarian food and energy supplies. Stop threats of use of force Calling Cuba’s revolutionary government “authoritarian” and labeling the country as a “sponsor of terrorism,” successive US administrations have tried to stage “regime change” in the country through covert and overt means, completely disregarding the Cuban people’s right to self-determination and their own obligations under international law. The Trump administration, after declaring Cuba “an unusual and extraordinary threat” last year, tightened the blockade and has even threatened to launch military operations against the country. It has demanded the Cuban government make policy changes based on Washington’s wishes. During the ongoing midterm campaign, Trump has reportedly claimed that the war against Cuba was imminent and can begin the moment the US armed forces were free from the war against Iran. Cuba has rejected US allegations and refused to surrender its sovereignty despite threats of war. Apart from providing humanitarian aid, China has also warned against such threats of military interventions raising the issue on various international forums, including the UN. Asking the Trump administration to “heed the call for justice from the international community,” Guo Jiakun reiterated on Thursday the Chinese demand that “the US stop all forms of coercion and pressure on Cuba, including through the threat of force.” Guo also reiterated that “China will continue firmly supporting Cuba’s just effort for safeguarding national sovereignty and dignity, and opposing external interference and embargo.” The reiteration of Chinese support follows its earlier pronouncement of support to Cuba’s revolutionary government “no matter how the international landscape evolves.” China, while observing 66 years of diplomatic relations with Cuba last month, had claimed that the “socialist development path” suited Cuba’s national conditions and helped in safeguarding its national sovereignty and opposing external interference.” Recognizing how Cuba was the first Latin American country to recognize the People’s Republic of China in 1960, Guo Jiakun claimed that, in recent years, the two countries have made “sustained and steady progress” in building a “community with a shared future.”

articles.title: “Democracy Itself Is on the Ballot”: Voters Weigh 150+ Ballot Initiatives, from Wealth Tax to Abortion
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : It’s Election Day across the United States, following the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. The group Open Secrets projects spending will reach nearly $12 billion. The New York Times reports the trillionaire Elon Musk has spent almost half a billion dollars, $474 million, in an attempt to help Republicans keep control of the House and Senate. On the campaign trail, Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico blasted Elon Musk’s role supporting his rival. REP . JAMES TALARICO : I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record. That is the contrast in this race. This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want a senator who serves you or who serves megadonors. And Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor. Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat in Texas. AMY GOODMAN : While James Talarico spoke in Austin, Texas, his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, campaigned in Allen, Texas. ATTORNEY GENERAL KEN PAXTON : That’s who he is. No matter how many commercials he runs lying about his record, James Talarico, simply put, is a democratic socialist, just like AOC and just like New York Mayor Mamdani. As a matter of fact, in his own words, he called Mandamini — Mamdani a template for future American politicians. I do not think that’s going to sit well with Bob Hall. AMY GOODMAN : In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed held a rally in Royal Oak Monday, one day after his Democratic primary challenger Haley Stevens endorsed Republican former Congressman Mike Rogers. Abdul El-Sayed focused in part on affordability. DR. ABDUL EL- SAYED : Shouldn’t be this hard to afford a second bag of groceries. Shouldn’t be this hard to pay your rent. Shouldn’t be this hard to fill up your tank. And it shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world. Shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money is going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids. It shouldn’t be this hard. AMY GOODMAN : Meanwhile, Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers campaigned in Rochester Hills. MIKE ROGERS : This election was never about how someone prayed. Never. It was always about how you think and what your philosophy and what your ideology is. And we would defend that. My entire family would defend your right to pray the way you want, and I’d go to the ends of the Earth to make sure that happened. But what it wasn’t — what it was about is that angry divisiveness that decided a certain segment of our society is the cause of all the ills in our community. AMY GOODMAN : While Senate, House and governor races have dominated news coverage, it’s not just candidates on today’s ballot. We’re going to turn first to look at some of the notable ballot initiatives, including a one-time tax on billionaires in California. It’s known as Proposition 40. We’re joined by Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. Chris, thanks so much for joining us. You know, people go to the polls. They’re hearing nonstop about the candidates. And then they’re faced, in some cases, with a number of ballot initiatives, and they’re not sure how to vote. But if you can talk about what are the ballot initiatives across the country? We’re talking about in, what, almost 40 states, over 145 ballot initiatives that people will be voting on, whether they understand them or not. CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : That’s exactly right. You know, this is a consequential election, and voters are going to be able to vote on democracy itself, whether they can participate in elections, how congressional districts are drawn, whether they will have autonomy of their own bodies. And our economy is on everybody’s minds, and that is going to be before voters, too, especially tax revenue measures that will determine whether we have the funding for public schools, for public goods, for public transportation. It’s an incredibly important election, and voters have the opportunity to take power into their own hands and improve the material conditions of their lives. AMY GOODMAN : You’ve said that what we’re seeing through the ballot process is part of rising authoritarianism. Can you explain? CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : Yeah. So, what we have been seeing through the initiative process is an attack on the will of the people. And direct democracy itself is on the ballot this year. Quite frankly, politicians are not happy with the power that people have demonstrated at the ballot box, and they are retaliating against voters right now to prevent them from exercising their voices. In competitive authoritarianism, they don’t cancel democracy outright, but they change the rules. They rig the system in favor of extremist lawmakers and special interests to weaken the power that we have in our democracy. And that’s because we’re winning. AMY GOODMAN : So, let’s talk specifics. You know, it’s very interesting when we look at the role of the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk, that he spent close to half a billion dollars on the election cycle across the country. And this record $12 billion is spent on the election, according to Open Secrets. Start in California, and talk about Proposition 40, and then talk about what are the efforts around the country to deal with money and money in politics. CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : Yeah. So, Prop 40 is a one-time, like you said, 5% tax on the assets of billionaires, and it’s expected to generate an estimated $100 billion to fund the state’s public health programs, education, food assistance and more. That’s something that impacts people’s daily lives. And it’s intended to fill massive funding gaps that have let fall because of the federal funding cuts that we are seeing across the country. It applies only to Californians with a net worth of at least $1 billion. That’s about 200 individuals with a combined wealth of $2 trillion. We have heard all election cycle — right? — of how much people want money out of politics, and they want billionaires to pay a fair share so that all of us can benefit in this country. AMY GOODMAN : Can you talk about what states are voting rights most contested? And talk specifically about specific ballot initiatives that you’re following in different states. CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : Yeah. I mean, we are seeing this is the first election after the Callais decision, after 60 years of the Voting Rights Act, and so democracy itself is on the ballot. You know, we have campaign finance reform. Michigan has Proposal 2, that will ban regulated utilities and block corporations from political campaigns. We have voter ID on the ballot in states like California. We have proof of citizenship. In Missouri, we have redistricting and overturning that gerrymandered maps that we’ve heard in the news, and it has gone up to the Supreme Court, I think, three times. So, really, across the country, democracy is on the ballot, including direct democracy itself. Like I said before, elected officials are not happy with us exercising our power, so in states like North Dakota, South Dakota are trying to raise the threshold so that we can exercise our ability to put issues on the ballot. AMY GOODMAN : Talk about the number of ballot initiatives for campaign finance reform. CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : So, we have Michigan’s Proposal 2 that I already mentioned. And then, Montana would also ban corporations, trade association and other, what they call, artificial persons from contributing to candidates, political parties or ballot measure campaigns themselves. AMY GOODMAN : And can you talk about initiatives seeking to expand reproductive rights? CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : Yeah. So, we are continuing the trend to protect our reproductive freedom across the country — Nevada, Virginia, Idaho. And it’s just really exciting that we are continuing to have this opportunity. And then, in one state, you know, it’s really important to really look at Missouri this year. Not only are they trying to overturn what the voters voted for in 2024 to restore reproductive freedom, they’re also going after gender-affirming care. AMY GOODMAN : Well, let’s talk about gender-affirming care. Talk about trans rights around the country and how they’re being dealt with through the ballot initiative process. CHRIS MELODY FIELDS FIGUEREDO : So, in five states, there are seven proposals that will attack transgender youth and their families. These are sports bans. These are bans on gender-affirming care. This is in Colorado, Arizona, Nebraska, Washington. And these are really, really important. This is our opportunity to ensure that we protect transgender youth and their families, and prevent government from really invasive procedures that will harm especially girls in our states. AMY GOODMAN : Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, I look forward to talking to after Election Day to find out how these initiatives fared. Chris is the executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. Oh, and tune in tonight for Democracy Now! 's four-hour live election night special , starting at 8 p.m. Join me and Juan González and Nermeen Shaikh and Anjali Kamat and many guests around the country as we stream live at democracynow.org and on our YouTube channel . And you can check your local Democracy Now! station for listings. That's 8 p.m. to midnight Eastern Time. Coming up, we look at Election Protection. We’ll speak with the NAACP on the group’s attempt to block the Trump administration from deploying a thousand federal agents to polling sites across the country. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “I Only Ask God,” popularized by Mercedes Sosa, performed by the Chilean American musician and producer Nicolás Jaar in our Democracy Now! studios. To see our interview with him and his performance, go to democracynow.org.

articles.title: Election Protection: NAACP Warns of Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Agents to the Polls
articles.content: As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP , which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls. The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

articles.title: Democratic Socialists on the Rise: Darializa Avila Chevalier & Claire Valdez Set to Win House Seats
articles.content: New York City is preparing to send two DSA members, presumptive election night winners Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, to Capitol Hill. DSA -backed candidates made historic gains in this year’s Democratic primaries, with at least five expected to join current DSA members Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in the House. But can socialism really make headway in the halls of Congress? Democracy Now! fellows Amba Guerguerian and Diego Ramos report. “Our task is going to be winning our colleagues over to our position and finding common ground,” Valdez tells Democracy Now! “Some of the most popular policies in our country’s history have been socialist policies,” says Avila Chevalier. “They have been the things that working people have organized for and won.”

articles.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for “Terrorizing Our Communities”: Marisa Franco of Mijente
articles.content: In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump. We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

articles.title: Students Celebrate Lula’s Victory and Denounce Violence Against Indigenous Peoples
articles.content: One week after the historic victory of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of the 2026 elections, the National Union of Students is holding nationwide mobilizations this Sunday, November 1. The rallies were titled “Brazil with an ‘S’” (“Brasil com S”). The actions came in response to statements made by supporters of defeated far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who questioned the election results. Beyond celebrating Lula’s win, the mobilizations also denounced and condemned the attacks against Indigenous peoples following the election. According to Brazil’s largest Indigenous organization, the Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, APIB, there have been more than 30 reports of violence against Indigenous individuals since the election. For Camila Moraes, secretary-general of the National Union of Students, the events that have unfolded since the election on Sunday, October 25, underscore the need for ongoing, permanent mobilization. “Today must also be a day of struggle,” she told Brasil de Fato . “A day to denounce the attacks and threats that the far-right continues to pose to the Brazilian people. We are seeing this in the attacks against Indigenous peoples, workers, and students, which amount to clear political intimidation. That is why I believe it is essential that we remain in a state of permanent mobilization, occupying the streets and, above all, organizing ourselves politically.” The president of the National Union of Students, Bianca Borges, participated in the demonstration at Praça Roosevelt, in the city of São Paulo. In a social media post, she emphasized the importance of sustained mobilization to ensure the stability of the Lula administration while also condemning the violence directed at Indigenous peoples following the election. “We have also gathered to denounce serious instances of political violence, including those targeting Indigenous communities,” she wrote. The ‘Brazil with an S’ mobilization took place this Sunday in Maceió, Manaus, Goiânia, Cuiabá, São Luís, Belém, Recife, Rio de Janeiro, Porto Alegre, São Paulo, Brasília, and Maringá.

articles.title: Special issue on Strategy: Call for website papers to continue the debate
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: The latest issue of Historical Materialism, a Special Issue on Strategy (Volume 33, Issue 4), aims to help reopen the strategic debate at a particularly complex time where challenges are mounting. The issue, naturally, does not cover all potential areas of strategic thinking and raises more questions than answers. It is a further step in an open discussion that needs to be continued. For this reason, with the aim of deepening the debate, we are launching a call for website papers, as a second phase of our strategic discussion. We are seeking contributions that we will run on our website ( www.historicalmaterialism.org ) that explicitly engage with one or many of the articles in the special issue, either in full or in part. Submissions: We are looking for full-length articles, to assess their suitability for publication. However, we are also open to receiving abstracts and proposals yet to be developed. As we receive proposals, we will assess them and, if accepted, publish them in due course. Please send articles or proposals to: info@historicalmaterialism.org Please indicate in the subject of the email that it is for the ‘Strategy Website CFP’ Deadline: The call for papers remains open for the time being, with no set end date. You can see the Table of Contents of the Special issue here: https://www.historicalmaterialism.org/journal/volume-33-issue-4-2025/ And the editorial introduction: Special Issue on Strategy – Josep Maria Antentas and Panagiotis Sotiris https://brill.com/view/journals/hima/33/4/article-p3_1.xml?srsltid=AYCX9vKgj7I4AfrmxlWYNIOGm1lltQpLpKYVenW0HPkQN-fo8f8kIQ2N&ebody=full%20html-copy1 The post Special issue on Strategy: Call for website papers to continue the debate appeared first on Historical Materialism .

articles.title: The Bund, anti-Zionism and the Jewish Left
articles.author: Janey Stone
articles.content: W ho would have imagined a few years ago that masses of people around the world would be reading, praising, arguing over, and condemning a book about an obscure Jewish socialist organization that effectively came to an end nearly 80 years ago? 1 https://bookmarks.reviews/reviews/all/here-where-we-live-is-our-country-the-story-of-the-jewish-bund/ A book about an uncompromisingly anti-Zionist organization? Who would have imagined such a book having rave reviews in the New York Review of Books 2 Adam Hochschild, “A Dream of a Socialist Commonwealth”, New York Review of Books, 28 May 2026; https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/05/28/a-dream-of-a-socialist-commonwealth-the-jewish-bund/ and The New York Times and being on the latter’s bestsellers list? 3 Max Strasser, “What Does Judaism Look Like Without Zionism?” New York Times, April 6, 2026; https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/06/books/review/here-where-we-live-is-our-country-molly-crabapple.html The Israeli state is carrying out a genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank, and increasing apartheid laws inside Israel. Not only does the world stand by and allow this—the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia (where I live) support, arm, and encourage the Israeli government, and succumb to pressure to cancel and criminalize pro-Palestinian activity. The conflation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism means not just a distortion of Zionism and what it stands for, but a loss of the historical reality of antisemitism. It also results in a distortion of Jewish history, a loss of the history of the majority of European Jews of the first half of the twentieth century, who were socialists, not Zionists. At a time like this, we need more than ever books that rediscover the other Jewish tradition, the history of radical struggle, opposition to Zionism, and socialism. The General Jewish Labour Bund in Lithuania, Poland, and Russia, generally known as the Jewish Labor Bund or just simply the Bund, was founded in 1897 in Vilna (Vilnius, now in Lithuania) in the tsarist empire. It is one of the most important but least recognized socialist organizations in Europe. In its early years, the Bund was revolutionary. It was the first socialist group to turn away from narrow circle work to agitation among workers in the late nineteenth century. It was also the first organization in Russia to implement many of the features we see today as characteristic of the revolutionary party: an agitational paper, professional revolutionaries, and the need for the party to be rooted among workers. The Bund also took the lead in organizing systematic self-defense against pogroms, which were endemic in the tsarist empire. Because of its resources and organizational skills, the Bund was central to organising the First Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) in 1898. By the Second Congress in 1903, it had 30,000 members, compared to 8,400 total for the other affiliates. Before the 1905 Revolution in Russia, one third of the prisoners in the Siberian labor camps were Bundists, and the party played a key role in that revolution. At the 1903 Congress, the Bund opposed Vladimir Lenin’s concept of the party. However, after the 1917 revolution, a sizable group broke away from the Bund and joined the revolutionary movement. The remaining Bund organization relocated to newly independent Poland, where it affiliated with the Second International. But there was little scope for reformist careerism under Józef Piłsudski’s authoritarian regime, and even less during the increasingly fascist period after he died in 1935. Subservience did not save the Polish Communist Party from destruction by Joseph Stalin. With Trotskyism virtually nonexistent, many of the best working-class activists were to be found in the Bund and in the Polish Socialist Party, also a member of the Second International. As they had done previously, the Bund continued its working-class-based activities, organizing workers into trade unions and leading self-defense groups against increasing fascist antisemitism. During World War II, the Bund also played a critical role in resistance to the Nazis, most notably during the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in April 1943. So much of this story appears to have been forgotten or relegated to footnotes. While there is a significant body of literature on the Bund, it has been treated as a niche topic, one for specialists in Jewish history. In Here Where We Live Is Our Country , Molly Crabapple has written a work of popular history. Although the author has undertaken original archival research, the book is unapologetically non-academic. To read it is more like reading a novel, a thriller, or a family saga. It is a page-turner, with a large cast of actors and vigorously drawn characters. Events are fast-paced, and the story unfolds against a backdrop of wars, revolutions, civil unrest, and local conflicts. Above all, this is a book about people’s personal experience. Crabapple is a visual artist, and reading this book is like watching a series of vignettes passing before your eyes. Central is her great-grandfather Sam Rothbort, who at 15 became an activist Bundist in the small town of Volkovysk (present-day Belarus). Rothbort participated in Bund-led strikes and gatherings in the forests, but eventually fled to the United States in 1904. Crabapple never knew her great-grandfather, but she did have a wonderful source of material in a shoe box of memorabilia, handwritten memoirs, and hundreds of paintings he left behind. This treasure trove inhabits the book almost as a living entity. Throughout the book, she draws on memoirs, letters, and personal accounts of many Bundists, men and women, young and old, leaders and rank-and-file members. She shows them to us as living human beings who were active players in history. Far from using an authorial distance and objectivity, Crabapple tries to enter the minds of her protagonists, to write subjectively. She speculates about how individuals must have felt and thought. Here is an example from the 1905 Revolution, sparked by the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin. Crabapple creatively describes the experiences of the Bundist soap box orator Anna Lipshitz: Soon, to move between neighbourhoods, Anna would have had to weave around overturned tramcars and slip behind barricades…She would have witnessed the beatings of police officers…and likely heard the explosion of anarchist bombs. It must have thrilled her. This moment was meant to be hers… Anna Lipshitz heard the news alongside the rest of the city. A battleship named Potemkin had just dropped anchor…It was flying a red flag. Hoarse, bleary, her dress stiff with dried sweat, Lipshitz would have pulled herself off the floor of her safe house and joined the crowds clambering toward the port. The ship gleamed like a dream. It is this sort of creative writing that animates this book, bringing to life the experience of revolution, war, and pogroms in a deeply effective way. We know, without it being articulated, that the dream that ends this passage is the possibility of a new world, one that inspired many participants in the revolution. Some reviews have criticized this approach. But in my view, Crabapple’s use of this form of creative nonfiction is valid, as long as it’s clear what is actually factually based and what is imagined by the author. The book offers something sometimes lacking in historical writing, and helps the reader imagine historical events as they were lived. It gives the sense that revolutionaries and socialists are actual human beings with enthusiasms and foibles, strengths and doubts, dreams and hopes. And that they live without the benefit of hindsight and the analytical books that came after them. The personal experience approach takes us to a particular time and place, and gives the reader the feeling that they are accompanying the protagonists on this journey. For example, when the Nazis invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, there were scenes of chaos. Crabapple brings these to life through realistic detail: the scramble to get news, organize meetings, make decisions, find food, locate relatives, and organize transport and visas. Their agonised debates: “All around Warsaw, rank-and-file Bundists were making similar calculations. Should they stay or run?” Crabapple does not take a position on this. She simply describes the dilemma. The events of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943 are already well-documented, but Crabapple gives us telling details. On the day it started, April 19, the Jewish Combat Organization battle squads mobilized at 2.00 am. “From balconies and windows, the fighters watched the nazis goose-step down Nalewki Street, singing a cheerful march. [Marek] Edelman had taken care to dress well that night, in a red angora sweater and two leather bandoliers, crossed like Pancho Villa. As he saw the convoy enter the ghetto, he imagined the Germans’ thoughts.” We know quite a bit about Edelman, who is famous for his account of the Warsaw Ghetto. 4 Marek Edelman, The Ghetto Fights , Bookmarks 2014 (and many other editions). But who knew he was wearing a red angora sweater at that moment? The book is enlivened on every page by similar less well-known details. Viktor Alter, who “liked the ladies,” was nicknamed “the Cary Grant of labor.” Bernard Goldstein is well-known for strong links to the criminal underworld, but he showed a softer side while in hiding during the Uprising, when he gave a young couple privacy in his apartment. Sophia Dubovna, when young, had a crush on the family maid (Sophia came from a rich family) and had briefly dated the right-wing Zionist Vladimir Jabotinsky. In 1934 she gave talks about love and sex at the Bund youth group, Tsukunft (Future). As a small child, Edelman had attended protests on the shoulders of comrades, “red flag in his tiny fist.” The accounts of pogroms and the suffering and destruction in the book show very vividly what antisemitism actually is historically. In so doing, they reveal contemporary attempts to reduce the concept of antisemitism to uncomfortable feelings in the presence of political slogans or keffiyehs as a horrifying trivialization of the historical oppression of Jews. The wonderful politics of the Bund shine throughout the book: its internationalism, its commitment to fighting antisemitism and to self-defense, to struggle, and to the working class. While the Zionists argued that antisemitism could never be defeated and so advocated emigration, the Bund promoted remaining and fighting against their oppression. But they took it even further. Using a biblical comparison, one Bundist declared that Jews should “stay and fight there, amongst the Egyptians, until they won a freedom that encompassed even their oppressors.” Bund leader Henryk Erlich made a similar argument. In 1937, against a backdrop of rising antisemitism and daily attacks by Polish fascists, increasing immiseration, and a clearly imminent war, Erlich urged his audience to look past their own concerns: You must briefly step out of the confines of your Jewish misery… Look about and you will see– the Jews are not the only ones who are suffering. The overwhelming majority in the country, whether Poles, Ukrainians, Jews, or others, is suffering from the economic crisis…scarcely able to eke out a daily existence. Shift your gaze beyond the borders of Poland toward the wide world and you will see: Seventy million people are languishing under the heavy boot of Hitlerism. Not only the 500,000 Jews – the whole German people has been transformed into a nation of slaves… Forty million Italians have been turned into a footstool for the ‘great’ Mussolini… millions of working people in other, smaller countries which have become areas of reaction are sunk in privation and bondage. Chaim Weizmann, leader of the World Zionist Federation in the interwar years, wrote in 1903 that their hardest struggle everywhere was conducted against the Bund. In return, the Bund described Zionism as “the most evil enemy of the organized Jewish proletariat.” In 1933, Erlich wrote: If Jewish nationalism, as a general rule, is not bloodthirsty, this is only out of necessity, not virtue; if an appropriate opportunity arose, Jewish nationalism would show its sharp teeth and nails no less than the nationalisms of other nations. No we are not a chosen people. Our nationalism is just as ugly, just as harmful, and has the same inclination to fascist debauchery as the nationalisms of other nations. In an open letter in 1938, Erlich summarised how they were the party that truly fought for the Jewish people: they had organized self-defense groups in tsarist Russia and in Poland, called protest strikes against pogroms, and argued against attempts to deport Jews. In relation to Palestine, he wrote: If a Jewish state should arise in Palestine, its spiritual climate will be: eternal fear of the external enemy (Arabs); eternal struggle for every bit of ground with the internal enemy (Arabs); and an untiring struggle for the extermination of the language and culture of the non-Hebraized Jews of Palestine… Is this a climate in which freedom, democracy and progress can grow?… Indeed, is it not the climate in which reaction and chauvinism ordinarily flourish? Concentrating on personal experience gives Here Where We Live Is Our Country strengths. But the method also has its weaknesses. Foremost is a lack of analysis. One should not read this book expecting an evaluation of the 1905 Revolution, the Bolshevik/Menshevik split, the role of the soviets in the 1917 revolutions, the growth of Stalinism, the civil war, the coming to power of the Nazis, or the causes of World War II. This is not the book’s objective, and these matters are very well covered elsewhere, but the lack of context is at times frustrating. While Crabapple features quotes and summaries of discussions, I wanted her book to engage more fully with the organizing principles and politics of the Bund. Consider the seminal event when the Bund sided with the Mensheviks in the famous split in 1903. Crabapple is dismissive: “Medem ruefully listened to rumors that the Iskrites had begun to fracture over the question of party membership. Should the RSDLP be a mass party of workers, as Martov envisioned? Or should it be the top-down conspiracy Lenin wanted, in which a central committee commanded and a full-time cadre obeyed? ‘Lenin had bared his teeth,’ Medem wrote.” Crabapple goes on to describe Lenin’s “personality traits that would shape the coming century.” Quoting Medem, she concludes Lenin resembled “a crafty Russian grain dealer… When you speak to him, he looks at you with his small eyes…(and) cunning devilish smile.” As Donny Gluckstein asks, “whether or not that characterisation was true, was Lenin right to believe a decentralised RSDLP facing the most centralised authoritarian state in the world was ‘a recipe for failure’?” 5 Donny Gluckstein, International Socialism Journal (forthcoming). Nathaniel Flakin also points out how the focus on Lenin’s personality prevents Crabapple from seriously grappling with the Bund’s political weaknesses and strategic mistakes. 6 Nathaniel Flakin, https://www.leftvoice.org/bundism-zionism-bolshevism/ . The concentration on personal experience also results in a lack of appreciation of collective experience and of competing social forces. This is particularly obvious in the account of the 1905 Revolution, in which her depiction of the turning of the tide is graphic but occurs for no apparent reason. The same happens with the growth of antisemitism in interwar Poland. This lack of social context results in an absence that is significant. Although the Bund became the leading Jewish organisation in Poland, it was not the only outlet for Jewish radicalism: Jews were prominent in other Left organizations. There was significant Jewish membership in the Polish Communist Party and the Polish Socialist Party. The left Zionist group Poale Zion joined in self-defense groups. None of this appears in the book. Here Where We Live Is Our Country has been rightly celebrated for its account of the Bund’s commitment to “Doykait” (“hereness”), meaning that Jews should not go elsewhere to escape discrimination but were entitled to equal rights and justice wherever they lived. Most writers seem to assume this meant that the Bund itself could be at home in any country. Yet it is abundantly clear that, although they were internationalist in spirit, the Bund’s roots were essentially in the Eastern European Yiddish-speaking working class, in particular in Poland by the 1930s. The Bund did not, in fact, transplant well. In the United States, with its more than two million Jewish immigrants, the Bund organization was small, mostly active in raising money to send to Europe and in the welfare-oriented Workman’s Circle and focusing mainly on cultural work and the promotion of the Yiddish language. While Bundists were likely involved in the mass strikes among Jewish clothing workers in New York before World War II, among which socialists were very active, the Bund played no clear role as an organization. Although there were individual Bundists in the United Kingdom who participated in a range of activities with other socialists, their work concentrated on collecting money for Poland and promoting Yiddish education. 7 Benjamin Nadel, “Bundism in England”, Jewish Socialist Group, Marxist Internet Archive, https://www.marxists.org/subject/jewish/jsg-bundism-uk.pdf The story is similar in Australia. This explains why the book ends when it does. The Holocaust destroyed the Bund’s roots among the Yiddish-speaking Jewish working class of Eastern Europe. As the war-torn regions of Europe slowly reorganized after 1945, the remaining Bund members tried for a time to hold on to their principled politics, particularly anti-Zionism. In two articles in 1948, the Bund leadership warned its readers that “the partition of Palestine and the creation of an independent Jewish State would lead to a new catastrophe, not only for the Jews in Palestine but for the Jews all over the world” and “the country became from the very start a source of Irredentist movements, Jewish-Arab conflicts, and an open threat of war.” 8 “Jewish Labor Bund and the Jewish-Arab war in Palestine”, The Jewish Labor Bund Bulletin , April 1948 pp3-5; https://www.marxists.info/subject/jewish/bund-bulletin/one-4.pdf. “The Jewish Labor Bund and the state of Israel”, The Jewish Labor Bund Bulletin , August-September 1948 pp 1-4; https://www.marxists.info/subject/jewish/bund-bulletin/one-8-9.pdf.p These articles generated a “veritable deluge” of condemnation from the entire Jewish press and the Jewish community as traitors. The Bund response was to argue, “We shall not be diverted by any temporary nationalist trend.” 9 “ We will not be bulled”, The Jewish Labor Bund Bulletin , August-September 1948 p 4; https://www.marxists.info/subject/jewish/bund-bulletin/one-8-9.pdf Unfortunately, the trend was not temporary. With the state of Israel firmly established, and the core organization in Poland destroyed, remnant groups in other countries faced a dilemma. The historian of the post-war Bund, David Slucki, shows how the movement came to a pragmatic accommodation with Zionism. 10 David Slucki, “The Bund abroad in the postwar Jewish world”, Jewish Social Studies , Vol 16, No 1, 2009, pp 111-144. Paradoxically, new international organizing principles allowed the local Bund groups to focus more on local activities, where they tended to straddle “the divide between mainstream Jewish communities and the non-Jewish socialist left.” Despite continued talk about socialism, bundists in the post–World War II era now saw “cultural continuity as their chief mission.” Thus, despite the formal opposition to Zionism, pragmatism led to an accommodation with Zionism, leading Bundists in Australia and elsewhere to send money to Israel. The political consequences became evident following the events of October 2023. Although some members of the Australian Bund are conspicuous and principled supporters of Palestine, the organisation has forefronted defense of Israel, publishing only three very short and weak statements (and none since 2025). 11 https://www.bundist.org/post/statement-on-events-in-gaza ; https://www.bundist.org/post/statement-enough ; https://www.bundist.org/post/statement-regarding-the-ongoing-horror-in-gaza. Writers associated with the Bund have even criticized Crabapple’s book as seeking to “delegitimise Israel” and even as “hijacked by anti-Zionists.” 12 Allan Preis, “The Bund Lives”, 20 July 2026 https://michaelgawenda.substack.com/p/the-bund-lives . It is sad to see contemporary Bundists repudiating their own history. 13 Janey Stone, “The International Jewish Labor BUND and the State of Israel”, Verso blog, 12 March 2025 https://www.versobooks.com/en-gb/blogs/news/the-international-jewish-labor-bund-and-the-state-of-israel-1?srsltid=AfmBOoqwvfG38HoXxzCSde4smFpBwKNyL929gYVG_m05MSqmf_bGmnFF But this history remains available to the rest of us. Its existence and predominance stand against the Zionist claims to represent Jews historically. The Bund’s internationalism and its position on Zionism prior to 1948 are beacons to contemporary anti-Zionists. And it’s clear that people are responding to this beacon. Jacobin applauds what it sees as the Bund’s “growing relevance,” 14 Grant Morgan, “The Jewish Labor Bund Stood Against Zionism”, Jacobin 22 April 2026; https://jacobin.com/2026/04/jewish-labor-bund-crabapple-review/ noting that where “the Bund has long been regarded as a historical artifact, it’s now reasserting itself as a living tradition.” New groups are springing up under the auspices of a body called the International Jewish Labor Bund (IJLB), 15 Joseph Mogul, “The Bund is Back”, The Progressive Magazine , March 31, 2026, https://progressive.org/latest/the-bund-is-back-mogul-20260331/ ; International Jewish Labor Bund Website https://jewishbund.org/ following its declaration in 2023. 16 “Today We Remake the Jewish Labor Bund”, https://derbund.org/#today-we-remake-the-jewish-labor-bund There are now 11 chapters or organizing committees in the United States and six in Europe, 17 https://jewishbund.org/chapters plus an online journal, Der Spekter. 18 https://www.derspekter.org/?shem=aimgspe (Interestingly, the remnant groups in Australia and elsewhere are not part of this movement.) The renewed interest in the Bund, its history, and its ideas, not surprisingly, has not been welcomed by everyone. Many of the negative responses to the book are trifling. Objections to Crabapple’s Puerto Rican roots, questioning whether she really is Jewish, and her past work as a burlesque dancer have only added fuel to the fire. Not surprisingly, Zionists have led the counter-attack. Their responses are defensive, and often abusive. Their fire is directed not at the book’s primary readership, but at a Zionist audience among whom this book (or the publicity it has generated) might raise doubts. A review in Haaretz is typical. 19 Joseph Hillyard, “A Missed Opportunity to Learn From the Legacy of the Bund” Ha’aretz, September 18, 2026; https://www.haaretz.com/opinion/2026-09-18/ty-article-opinion/.premium/a-missed-opportunity-to-learn-from-the-legacy-of-the-bund/000001a0-b4db-d91d-afeb-fcdb5c980000?gift=8d084db683a8479ba5304dc323911bd1 One strategy is nit-picking very small errors: Eliezer Aryeh, for example, devotes several articles to a forensic analysis of Crabapple’s nearly 2,000 endnotes and comes up with four errors. 20 Eliezer Aryeh, “What the Footnotes Don’t Say: Here Where We Live Is Our Country gets the Bund right and Palestine wrong” and other articles, May 29 2026 and subsequent dates, https://eliezeraryeh.substack.com/archive?sort=new Others complain that Crabapple “oversimplifies,” is “selective,” or makes “no attempt at representing historical accuracy. Seth Mandel, a conservative anti-Trump Republican, hardly touches on the content of the book at all, but claims (without evidence and despite many of the rave reviews being written by Jews) that the prevailing opinion among Jewish writers is that Crabapple’s book “exhibited a heartfelt nostalgia for a time and place that never really existed…it is a fictional story.” 21 Seth Mandel, “So You Want To Be a Bundist”, Commentary 7/4/2026; https://www.commentary.org/seth-mandel/so-you-want-to-be-a-bundist/?shem=aimgspe Writing in the Jewish Review of Books , Allan Arkush goes further, claiming Zionism “has by and large been rooted in humanitarianism, led by noble men and women dedicated to constructing and sustaining a Jewish state for the benefit of their own beleaguered people and, indirectly, for others.” 22 Allan Arkush, “An Abusable Past”, Jewish Review of Books , Fall 2026; https://jewishreviewofbooks.com/jewish-history/20334/an-abusable-past/?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&fbclid=IwY2xjawUixP1leHRuA2FlbQIxMABwZG9mAWJyaWQRMU9rcld4elZHTjFpV01IdjRzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEeGMZdDT0dDz9ZAqrLpDKj2K2lAkxDIWrd8iO5N1lnIYFE9XL5FcUol7cmiVM_aem_hpiD7t7BnHx3PQckSppt1A The Wall Street Journal review, written by a British Trump supporter apparently with the use of AI, regurgitates standard support for Israel for a non-Jewish audience. 23 Dominic Green, “Here Where We Live is Our Country Review: Defiance in the Diaspora”, Wall Street Journal, July 14, 2026; https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/here-where-we-live-is-our-country-review-defiance-in-the-diaspora-4b2b2b88 This book is not an academic study. The bibliography is small. Crabapple certainly carried out extensive new archival research, resulting in fascinating personal detail about her protagonists. But the book is rightly focused on introducing the Bund to wider audiences. The need today is not for more academically rigorous studies, to be read only by a limited audience, but for the core ideas in this book—struggle, resistance, solidarity, social justice, and above all socialism—to be spread further. Whatever its limitations, Here Where We Live is our Country i s a wonderful new addition to the history of the Bund and, through this, to the broader tradition of Jewish radicalism and socialism of which it is a part. This history is a part of our collective story, and its legacy belongs to all of us. Read this book in that spirit. articles.title: Left parties in Pakistan rally in solidarity with Cuba
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Hundreds participated in a solidarity rally in Lahore, Pakistan, earlier this week, demanding an end to the oppressive decades-long US blockade and sanctions on Cuba and denouncing its targeting of Raul Castro, leader of the Cuban revolution and former president. The participants raised slogans throughout the rally proclaiming the death of US imperialism and its inhuman blockade against the socialist nation. They expressed solidarity with Cuba, its people, the government, and Raul Castro in their fight against US hegemonic endeavors. Hundreds of e-rickshaws decorated with red flags moved across Pakistan’s second largest city on Sunday. The riders of the rickshaws, which generally carry people going to work, were holding banners and posters displaying solidarity messages in Urdu, Cuban flags, and pictures of Raul Castro. The rally was jointly called by the Mazdoor Kisan Party (MKP) and the Punjab Rickshaw Union (PRU) on the eve of the annual UN General Assembly vote on Cuba. Cuba’s socialist revolutionary government has been facing US sanctions and blockade for decades now. The intensity of the blockade has increased since Donald Trump came to power for his second term in 2025 causing shortages of energy, food, and medicine to its population. The Trump administration has also issued indictments against Castro (95) with an official in Florida issuing an “arrest warrant” against him earlier this month. Washington’s illegal policies against Cuba, its government, and Castro have invited global condemnations. Several countries and groups across the world have organized Cuba solidarity events declaring that “Cuba is not alone.” Cuba is not alone The march in Lahore culminated in a meeting which was addressed by Taimur Rahman; general secretary of the MKP, Irfan Ali; leader of the PKU, and others. Speaking in the meeting, Rahman declared that “Cuba was not alone” in its fight against imperialism and hegemonic policies. The fight of the Cuban people against imperialism is a fight of all the working class across the globe. He extended the solidarity of Pakistan’s working classes and called for greater mobilizations in solidarity with the Cuban people. He also pointed out how the UNGA has repeatedly denounced the US policies towards Cuba. He noted that the overwhelming majority in the world are opposed to the inhuman US policies and underlined that the illegal US sanctions and criminal blockade have disrupted the normal life of millions of Cubans. “Cuba is facing a genocidal blockade by imperialism. They literally are trying to starve the people into submission,” Rahman said in a post on X following the UNGA vote. He also pointed out the criminality of the Trump administration and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in particular. The MKP reiterated its solidarity message during its annual meeting commemorating the historic anti-feudal struggles in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province on Wednesday. On Wednesday, the UNGA adopted a resolution demanding an end to the inhuman imperialist blockade and sanctions on Cuba with an overwhelming majority of 130 countries voting in favor and only 27 voting against. Defying pressure from the US, the majority of the countries in the UNGA, including Pakistan , have repeatedly voted on similar resolutions since the 1990s. Several leaders speaking during the discussion on the resolution earlier this week yet again highlighted how the US has disregarded the UN charter, international laws, and the will of the Cuban people in its attempts to seek dominance.

articles.title: War in Africa: the political economy of the richest continent in the world
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Mainstream news has rediscovered Africa, and it is recycling old narratives: armed conflict, state collapse, and humanitarian catastrophe. Tigray is at war again. Darfur and Kordofan bleed under the Rapid Support Forces. M23 carves up eastern Congo. Northern Mozambique is still emptying its villages. Across the Sahel, jihadist attacks and blockades strangle whole towns, and Somalia’s war grinds on into its fourth decade. All of this is real. People are dying, and millions are displaced. But why is the story always told the same way it was told in the 1990s and early 2000s, as a continent of chaos and hunger, a cautionary tale, an example of what not to be? As an African reporter who covers these wars, I read the briefings and explainers sent out to the world and often struggle to recognize the places they describe. Look at Sudan. Now one of the largest displacement crises in the world, routinely called “the forgotten war,” as if forgetting were something that happened to the press rather than something the press did. Congo is reported as “decades of ethnic violence” and “a complex web of armed groups,” while the minerals the rebels fight over, and who buys them, rarely make it into the analysis. Ethiopia’s wars become conflicts between ethnic groups – Amhara against Tigrayan, Tigrayan against Eritrean, as if history ended with ethnicity. Compare this to the attention, the maps, the expert panels and the explanations of strategy that the war in Ukraine receives every week. That framing does three things. It flattens very different histories into one image of “African violence.” It turns politics into ethnicity. And it blames a supposedly unique African corruption, as if corruption were not a global industry. What it hides is that one of the richest continents in natural resources is home to many of the poorest people in the world. This is no accident of culture. It is the result of imperialism, a word too often missing from these conversations. Read more: Over half of Africa’s population suffered from food insecurity: UN report The news files Africa’s wars in separate stories. Read together, they draw one map. In Sudan, gold from RSF-held mines flows to the United Arab Emirates. In eastern Congo, UN experts place Rwandan troops beside M23 , and coltan from mines such as Rubaya passes through Rwanda into the supply chains for phones and electric-car batteries. In Mozambique, Rwandan soldiers, with European Union funding, guard the Cabo Delgado region where TotalEnergies is developing its gas project. On the Red Sea, Egypt, the Gulf states and Washington compete for the coastline Ethiopia and Eritrea are fighting over, and in September the United States lifted sanctions on Eritrea to advance its interests there. Even peace follows the pattern; when Congo and Rwanda signed the Washington Accords in December 2025, Donald Trump announced American deals to unlock the region’s critical minerals. And the weapons? None of these armed groups manufactures its own. The permanent war economy of the West, and increasingly of the Gulf, needs markets and battlefields. Africa supplies both. The “identity” cover story This structure needs a cover story, and “tribe” is the oldest one. Identity is real, and people do mobilize through it. Yet it is telling that “tribe” is still the label reached for when these wars are analyzed. Look at the resources being fought over. Ethnicity might tell who fights whom. It does not explain why the fighting pays. Many of the identities now presented as ancient hatreds were hardened, and sometimes made, by colonial rule. In Rwanda, Belgian administrators turned the fluid categories of Hutu and Tutsi into racial classifications, stamped on identity cards from the 1930s, with rights and privileges attached to each. In Sudan, the division of Darfur into “Arab” and “African” owes as much to Khartoum’s arming of the Janjaweed in the 2000s as to any older history. Colonial and post-colonial states governed through ethnicity, and their successors still do. So, when coverage reaches for “tribe,” it does not just simplify. It takes a political product of the empire and presents it as the cause of the wars that the empire’s heirs now profit from. How the wealth leaves The word “imperialism” can sound like an accusation without a mechanism. But the mechanism is not hidden. It runs through ordinary channels. UNCTAD estimates that close to $89 billion leaves Africa every year as illicit capital flight, through trade mis-invoicing, tax evasion, and the export of extractive commodities. That is nearly as much as the continent receives in aid and foreign investment combined. Add the profits that multinational firms send home each year, and the picture of Africa as a charity case turns upside down. The continent is a net creditor to the world that lectures it. Debt finishes the job. Loans taken under pressure, often to service earlier loans, now absorb budgets that should go to clinics and schools. Across much of the continent, governments pay more in interest to foreign creditors than they spend on the health of their own people. A state that cannot pay soldiers, nurses or teachers is then called “fragile,” and its fragility becomes the excuse for the next intervention. How, then, should Africa’s wars be covered? Not by looking away from the suffering, but by refusing to treat it as natural or without history. Every report on a massacre in Darfur should say where Darfur’s gold goes. Every report on M23 should name the mines it holds and the countries its minerals pass through. Every report on a peace deal should ask who gains access to what. Name specific histories, specific companies and specific capitals, not a faceless “Africa.” These are the questions I try to bring to my own reporting, and the ones I would put to every newsroom that covers the continent. The popular sentiment among young African people is dignity and sovereignty. And sovereignty belongs to people, not to whichever general holds the capital. That is why those organizing from below deserve our attention even more. Grassroots movements and organizations, which have kept food, medicine, and political life going through the war, and the popular movements across the Sahel that demanded an end to foreign occupation. articles.title: Across the Red Sea, the wars feed each other
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: Sudan’s war is usually described as an African catastrophe, Yemen’s as an Arabian conflict, and the war around Iran as a Gulf crisis. Such divisions obscure the movement of weapons, money, soldiers, and commercial interests between them. Look from Africa’s Red Sea coast, and another picture emerges. These wars have distinct origins, but they increasingly sustain one another through military patronage, competition over ports, and the destruction of civilian livelihoods. The starting point must be Sudan’s people. The World Food Program currently estimates that 19.5 million face acute hunger, while around 8.6 million are internally displaced. It reports that sorghum prices are nearly three times higher than a year ago and wheat flour prices have almost doubled. Maritime disruption is raising fuel and fertilizer costs. Sudanese families therefore confront their own war and the economic consequences of wars across the water. The fighting that began in April 2023 between Abdel Fattah al-Burhan’s Sudanese Armed Forces and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo’s Rapid Support Forces grew out of from Sudan’s militarized political economy. Dagalo, commonly known as Hemedti, built his power through a paramilitary apparatus rooted in Darfur’s violence. Both military centers accumulated economic power and obstructed civilian democracy. Foreign intervention enlarged their capacity to destroy a country whose popular movement had demanded a different future. Yemen helped prepare this disaster. After Sudan joined the Saudi-led intervention in 2015, Sudanese soldiers, including large RSF contingents, crossed the Red Sea. The International Crisis Group’s 2019 investigation found that Hemedti supplied considerably more troops than the regular army and that his forces frequently occupied frontline positions. Poor families supplied recruits attracted by military earnings. An impoverished African population became a source of fighting labor for wealthy Gulf monarchies. That deployment strengthened Hemedti’s standing and external relationships. His forces acquired battlefield experience while he cultivated patrons beyond Sudan’s borders. The significance exceeds any individual payment or deployment. Gulf intervention helped a Sudanese commander consolidate an armed organization with resources and relationships outside civilian control. A war fought in Yemen contributed to the growth of a military center that would later wage war inside Sudan. The connection is direct and historical. Gold supplied another foundation. The UN Panel of Experts’ January 2024 report described gold as a continuing revenue source for Sudan’s warring parties and documented smuggling networks. One consignment linked to an RSF-associated trader reached Dubai through Port Sudan in May 2023. The panel also found that routes shifted towards Egypt after fighting began. This is a regional war economy, capable of changing its commercial pathways when circumstances require. Interventions in Sudan The UAE’s role requires scrutiny. Amnesty International reported in May 2025 that guided bombs and howitzers used by the RSF had almost certainly been re-exported through the Emirates. Its analysis examined identifiable weapons and munition remnants. Abu Dhabi denies supplying the RSF, but that denial must be recorded alongside the visual evidence. International arms suppliers also bear responsibility for preventing diversion into Sudan. An October 2026 European Union Agency for Asylum assessment describes reported RSF supply routes through eastern Chad, southeastern Libya, and northeastern Somalia. These routes connect Sudan’s interior to a much wider African geography. Airfields, border crossings, commercial intermediaries, and military patrons matter as much as formal alliances. Darfur cannot be protected while the networks replenishing armed groups remain intact. Nor can responsibility be confined to the men who pull the trigger. Saudi Arabia and Egypt, meanwhile, favor the Sudanese army, although their interests and policies differ. Riyadh combines mediation with support for the continuity represented by Burhan’s authorities, while Cairo regards Sudan’s territorial integrity and the survival of a central state as strategic concerns. These preferences do not make either government an advocate of Sudanese popular democracy. The danger is that negotiations become a bargain among military patrons over the country’s future. There is consequently no single Gulf policy towards Africa. Saudi and Emirati interests overlap, then collide. Sudan exposes these differences, as does Yemen. Nor does hostility towards Iran produce an uncomplicated regional division. Such relationships show how local military authorities seek assistance from different sources, while foreign governments calculate their interests separately in each theater. Their alignments are practical, contingent, and dangerous. The African coastline gives these relationships their strategic setting. Port Sudan connects a vast hinterland to the Red Sea. Further south, ports facing the Gulf of Aden offer access to shipping near Bab al-Mandab. Commercial investment can meet real development needs, but port contracts become politically combustible when combined with foreign security arrangements or agreements that bypass national institutions. Control of an entry point can shape an entire country’s economic options. Somalia has challenged this pattern. In a January interview with Al Jazeera, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Ali Mohamed Omar explained his government’s cancellation of agreements with the UAE. He accused Abu Dhabi of undermining Somali sovereignty through dealings with entities outside the federal government. He said military personnel and equipment should leave, while investments in Berbera and Bosaso required a legal settlement. These were Mogadishu’s stated demands, not proof that every arrangement immediately ended. The dispute reveals the African stakes of competition across the water. Somaliland and Puntland have their own political histories and interests, but outside powers can exploit disputes over authority to secure ports and military access. African sovereignty then becomes negotiable between external capitals and competing local authorities. What appears from abroad as logistical efficiency may appear locally as the fragmentation of the state and the loss of democratic control. Yemen provides a warning against assuming that such arrangements are permanent. One assessment records the collapse of much of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council’s territorial control in January 2026 after advances by Saudi-backed forces. Emirati troops withdrew, including from Socotra and Perim. Yet local allies retained influence. Withdrawal therefore changed the form and extent of Emirati power without demonstrating that Abu Dhabi had ceased to matter in Yemen. Renewed fighting now threatens the southern Red Sea. On October 29, Ansar Allah claimed attacks on Saudi refineries, an Aramco facility, and airports. Saudi authorities reported interceptions and limited casualties and damage from debris. On October 30, the coalition announced another interception towards the Mecca region, which Ansar Allah denied targeting that day. These competing statements establish escalation, but they cannot establish that every claimed target was struck. Saudi–Emirati rivalry nevertheless coexists with security cooperation. On October 7, the UAE Foreign Ministry condemned attacks on Saudi civilian and economic facilities and Saudi vessels in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. The two governments can oppose each other’s local partners while supporting each other against another adversary. Treating them as either a unified bloc or irreconcilable enemies conceals how intervention actually operates. The United States and Israel widened this system of insecurity through their war against Iran. The military escalation made countries already involved in African conflicts confront new threats at home. Yet their vulnerability has not dissolved their competing African ambitions. For Africa, the lesson is that dependence on outside military patrons imports their wider confrontations. A government seeking weapons for one battlefield may become entangled in struggles whose decisions are taken elsewhere, while its own population inherits the economic costs and the political dangers of those decisions for years afterwards. The war around Iran magnifies these dangers through the maritime economy. Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab are separate straits, but disruption at both strains connected trading systems. UNCTAD estimated in March that about one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade passes through Hormuz. Energy costs, insurance premiums, and freight charges transmit military escalation into agricultural costs. African countries experience this connection through import bills, shortages, and pressure on already restricted public finances. For a Sudanese farmer, these pressures arrive on top of displacement and lost harvests, and for neighboring countries sheltering refugees, they increase the cost of supporting people driven from their homes. The consequences extend far beyond the coastline. War damages production directly, then raises the price of restoring it. The same commercial system that facilitates the circulation of weapons becomes more expensive for those trying to move food and fertilizer. Diplomacy must address these connections without denying each conflict’s political roots. On October 20, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah had not responded to Tehran’s mediation offer. An understanding involving Washington and Tehran could reduce regional pressure, but it would not automatically settle Yemen’s struggles over government, territory, and resources. Likewise, a Saudi–Emirati accommodation would leave Sudan’s demand for civilian democracy unresolved. An African agenda for peace must therefore insist on halting external military supplies, protecting humanitarian routes, and defending sovereign control over ports and resources. Sudanese civilian organizations must have decisive political space in any settlement. The Red Sea should connect peoples through trade and cooperation, and its shores cannot be surrendered to arrangements in which African wealth pays for African destruction while outside powers negotiate their shares of the resulting ruin. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist. He is the author of forty books, including Washington Bullets, Red Star Over the Third World, The Darker Nations: A People’s History of the Third World, The Poorer Nations: A Possible History of the Global South, and How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, written with Grieve Chelwa. He is the executive director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, the chief correspondent for Globetrotter, and an editor at LeftWord Books (New Delhi). He also appeared in the films Shadow World (2016) and Two Meetings (2017). This article was produced by Globetrotter .
